title: What If the Moon Disappeared? The Full Story
lines: Tonight, the Moon is gone.
No explosion, no warning. It simply isn't there anymore.
What if the Moon disappeared? This is the full story, from the first dark night to millions of years later.
Some changes would hit right away. Others would take ages. And a few might surprise you.
First, let's meet what we'd be losing.
The Moon orbits about [384,400 kilometers](three hundred eighty four thousand, four hundred kilometers) away on average. That's roughly [239,000 miles](two hundred thirty nine thousand miles).
It's about [3,475 kilometers](three thousand four hundred seventy five kilometers) across, roughly a quarter of Earth's width.
And it has only about [1.2%](one point two percent) of Earth's mass. Earth is about [81](eighty one) times heavier.
Small as it is, it lights our nights, raises our tides, sets the rhythm for countless animals, and may even help steady our planet.
The first change is the one you'd notice right away: the night.
Moonlight is just sunlight bouncing off the Moon. Its surface reflects only about a tenth of the light that hits it, about as dark as worn asphalt.
The Sun is roughly [400,000](four hundred thousand) times brighter than a full Moon. Yet that faint glow is what lights up a moonlit night.
Without it, every single night would be as dark as the night of a new Moon.
From a dark place on a clear night, you'd see far more stars, and the Milky Way would stand out whenever it's above the horizon.
But for about a third of humanity, a [2016](twenty sixteen) study found, light pollution already hides the Milky Way. That wouldn't change.
Next, the oceans. Tides are the slow rise and fall of the sea, and the Moon is the main reason they happen.
The Moon pulls a little harder on the side of Earth facing it, and a little less on the far side. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges.
The Sun raises tides too, but its tide-raising force is a little less than half of the Moon's.
So without the Moon, only the Sun would raise tides, and they'd be roughly a third to half as big as today.
We'd also lose spring and neap tides. Today the biggest tides come at new and full Moon, and the smallest at the quarter Moons.
Without the Moon, that two-week rhythm would disappear.
And the strip of shore between high and low tide, home to tide pools and mudflats, would get much narrower.
And that's just the water. A lot of life runs on a Moon schedule.
On Australia's Great Barrier Reef, many corals spawn together, one to six nights after the full Moons of October, November and December.
Scientists found a light-sensing gene in corals that switches on under the faint blue light of the full Moon. It may help them keep time.
Lose the Moon, and that shared clock could fall out of sync.
Sea turtle hatchlings crawl toward the brightest horizon, which on a natural beach is the open sea.
Moonlight and starlight over the water help guide them. That's why bright beach lights can send them the wrong way.
Some African dung beetles roll their dung balls in straight lines by following polarized moonlight, a pattern about a million times dimmer than sunlight's.
One species can even steer by the Milky Way on moonless nights, the first animal known to do that.
Predators feel the Moon too. Lions hunt most successfully on the darkest nights, while many rodents and bats lie low when the Moon is bright.
In California, grunion fish ride the highest tides of the month onto beaches to lay their eggs, for a few nights starting at each full and new Moon.
Without the Moon, rhythms like these would have to change, or break.
We'd lose things that are part of human history, too.
The word month comes from the same old root as Moon. And the Islamic calendar still begins each month when the thin crescent is first seen.
Eclipses would end forever. No more total solar eclipses, and no more red lunar eclipses.

This August, a total solar eclipse crossed Greenland, Iceland and Spain. The next, in August [2027](twenty twenty seven), will cross southern Spain and North Africa, with over six minutes of totality near [Luxor](LUCK-sore), Egypt.
[12](Twelve) people have walked on the Moon, on six Apollo landings between [1969](nineteen sixty nine) and [1972](nineteen seventy two).
And this April, the four astronauts of Artemis Two flew around it, farther from Earth than any humans before them.
Now for the slow changes, the ones that would play out over millions of years.
Earth and the Moon actually orbit a shared balance point, about [4,700 kilometers](four thousand seven hundred kilometers) from Earth's center, still inside our planet.
That makes Earth wobble a little every month. Without the Moon, that wobble would simply stop.
The bigger question is Earth's tilt. Today our axis leans about [23.4](twenty three point four) degrees, and that tilt gives us our seasons.
Over the last million years, it has only drifted between about [22.1](twenty two point one) and [24.5](twenty four point five) degrees, in a cycle of about [41,000](forty one thousand) years.
Many scientists think the Moon helps keep that tilt steady.
In [1993](nineteen ninety three), a famous study found that without the Moon, Earth's tilt could swing chaotically, from almost zero to about [85](eighty five) degrees.

Later simulations found something much milder. The tilt would wander more than it [does](duz) today, but within a range of about [20 to 25](twenty to twenty five) degrees, over hundreds of millions of years.
Scientists still debate how much the Moon really matters. But more tilt means stronger seasons, so even a milder wander could reshape climates over very long times.
Earth's spin would change too. Right now, the tides act like a slow brake on our planet, and the Moon causes most of that braking.
Because of that braking, each century the day gets about two thousandths of a second longer.
The Sun's tides would keep slowing Earth, but much more gently, so our days would stretch far more slowly.
To see why the Moon matters so much, go back about four and a half billion years.
The leading idea is that a Mars-sized world, often called [Theia](THEE-uh), slammed into the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the debris.
Since then, its tides have been slowing us down. About [1.4](one point four) billion years ago, a day lasted just over eighteen hours.
And the Moon is still leaving. Lasers bounced off reflectors left by Apollo astronauts show it drifting away about [3.8](three point eight) centimeters a year.
That's only about an inch and a half a year, far too slow to lose it any time soon.
So the next time you look up, remember what the Moon gives us: lighter nights, bigger tides, a clock for life, and maybe a steadier world.
Thanks for watching, and follow for more what ifs!
